strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: the paper formalizes four physically motivated axioms (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, energy balance/passivity) and proves a local Jacobian-level reduction theorem showing that under these axioms, mesh dynamics must factor into a port-Hamiltonian form with a topology-fixed, signed-incidence conservative interconnection and separately learnable metric/dissipation operators. The full proof (Appendix A) is careful and the argument for why each axiom is necessary (via counterexamples/relaxations) is a nice touch.

The electromagnetism worked example (Appendix B) nicely illustrates that Maxwell's equations and topological invariants (discrete div B=0, charge-free div D=0) emerge as consequences of the theorem rather than being assumed, lending credibility to the abstract framework.

Extensive and carefully designed empirical validation: analytic plane-wave benchmarks (grid and Delaunay meshes), a dissipative/Rayleigh-damped variant, a multi-faceted physics-consistency battery (wave speed, canonical consistency, PDE residual, equipartition, momentum, vector-field alignment, amplitude/phase), three types of OOD generalization (frequency, resolution, parameter shift), a real dataset from The Well (acoustic scattering), a nonlinear state-dependent toy problem, a targeted ablation study isolating which axioms matter, and a computational cost analysis.

MeshFT-Net achieves consistently strong results across nearly all these settings, often by orders of magnitude in energy drift and physical-consistency diagnostics, while using dramatically fewer parameters (642 vs ~100k-200k) and lower latency/memory than baselines, supporting the practical value of the inductive bias.

The ablation study (Table 9) is a valuable sanity check that directly interrogates the theorem's necessity claims (breaking orientation, topology, metric positivity, or learning J directly) and shows measurable degradation consistent with the theory.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow relative to the motivating applications (fluid/solid mesh simulation à la MeshGraphNets): most experiments are on linear 2D plane-wave/wave-equation settings on regular or Delaunay meshes; the single nonlinear/state-dependent experiment is a small synthetic "shallow-water-style" toy problem rather than a realistic nonlinear PDE, so the paper does not convincingly demonstrate the approach on the complex, nonlinear, large-deformation problems that originally motivated learned mesh simulators.

The real-data validation (acoustic scattering from The Well) is comparatively thin: it presents only qualitative pressure-field snapshots (Fig. 3) without a quantitative table comparing MeshFT-Net against the same baselines used elsewhere (MGN, HNN, etc.), making it hard to assess relative real-world performance.

The main experiments adopt the state-independent, quadratic-storage simplification (Corollary 3.4) almost throughout, while the more general nonlinear/state-dependent formulation (Section 4 "General" case) is essentially only lightly touched by the small toy ablation in 5.5; this leaves a gap between the generality claimed by the theorem and what is actually validated.

Some baselines (e.g., PI-MGN) diverge (">100") in many OOD and physics-consistency conditions, which raises a question about whether baselines were adequately tuned/matched in capacity or training budget for a fully fair comparison, especially since MeshFT-Net uses orders of magnitude fewer parameters and a specialized symplectic integrator that baselines do not share architecturally.

The paper does not include a direct empirical comparison to the closely related data-driven exterior calculus approach (Trask et al., 2022), despite discussing it at length in related work, which would have been a natural and informative baseline given the topology-metric split shared by both methods.

The treatment of boundaries, external sources, and non-mesh-conforming heterogeneities is only briefly mentioned (e.g., sponge layers for open boundaries in the acoustic scattering experiment) without deeper theoretical or empirical exploration, leaving open how well the framework handles more complex boundary/source conditions common in real applications.

The manuscript is dense and notation-heavy (many appendices with lemmas/corollaries), which, combined with reliance on promised (not yet reviewed) supplementary code, makes full independent reproducibility somewhat harder to verify at this stage.

strengths: A genuine theoretical contribution: rather than positing a port-Hamiltonian template, the paper derives (Theorem 3.3, with a careful multi-lemma proof in Appendix B) that locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and an energy-balance/passivity condition together force the Jacobian of any admissible mesh dynamics to factor into a topology-fixed skew-symmetric incidence wiring plus a metric/dissipation part. This gives a principled, falsifiable rationale for the common DEC-style topology/metric split rather than assuming it outright.

Very extensive empirical program: analytic plane-wave tests on regular and Delaunay meshes, a dissipative benchmark, five/six physics-consistency diagnostics (wave speed, canonical consistency, PDE residual, equipartition, momentum, vector-field alignment), OOD shifts in frequency/resolution/wave-speed, a real dataset (The Well acoustic scattering), nonlinear/heterogeneous lattice and elasticity benchmarks, and multiple targeted ablations (topology-vs-metric separation, state-dependent coupling, and principle-level ablations that individually break orientation, topology, or metric positivity) that directly test the necessity of each theorem assumption.

Strong and fairly matched baseline suite (MGN, MGN-HP, HNN, PI-MGN, FNO, GraphCON) trained under identical protocols/integrators, which strengthens the comparative claims beyond a simple straw-man MGN comparison.

Reports computational cost (latency, memory, parameter count) showing large efficiency gains, and provides an EM-theory worked example (Appendix C) that grounds the abstract theorem in a concrete, checkable physical system (Maxwell's equations) with explicit topological invariants preserved.

Honest scoping of claims: the paper explicitly states the reduction is local/Jacobian-level and does not claim a single global port-Hamiltonian representation, and the appendix ablations test sharpness of each assumption rather than merely asserting it.
weaknesses: Nearly all quantitative benchmarks are synthetic problems (linear/near-linear wave equations, lattice oscillators) whose data-generating processes are essentially expressible within the exact DEC/port-Hamiltonian template the model imposes; this risks the strong numerical superiority being partly an artifact of matching the inductive bias to the data-generating structure rather than evidence of broader applicability to physics that is not naturally expressible this way (e.g., strongly nonlocal, advection-dominated, or turbulent phenomena).

The one real-world dataset (The Well acoustic scattering, Sec. 5.4) is evaluated only qualitatively (visual snapshots) with no quantitative table comparing MeshFT-Net against the baselines used elsewhere in the paper, leaving the central 'transfer to realistic data' claim less substantiated than the synthetic results.

Completeness of the local, permutation-equivariant linear basis in Lemma B.1 (restricted to {Id, A_k, D_{k-1}, D_k^T}) is asserted rather than rigorously justified via a representation-theoretic or exhaustive argument; a reader cannot easily verify that no other local, equivariant linear operators exist on general oriented complexes.

Experimental scale remains modest (grids up to 128×128, meshes with hundreds to a few thousand nodes), so scalability and behavior on large, high-resolution, or 3D meshes relevant to realistic engineering/scientific simulation remain unverified.
The abstract states 'the code is available at' with no actual link provided in the manuscript, undermining verifiable reproducibility at submission time.

Many reported metrics (e.g., Table 2, 4) lack variance/uncertainty estimates in the main text (only some appendix tables include std), making it harder to judge the significance of certain smaller gaps between MeshFT-Net and the strongest baselines (e.g., HNN in some columns).
